source.title: MonoLoss: A Training Objective for Interpretable Monosemantic Representations
source.authors: Ali Nasiri-Sarvi; A. Nguyen; H. Rivaz; Dimitris Samaras; M. Hosseini

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or cutoff; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures semantic consistency of vision-model representation dimensions with MonoScore and class purity, and tests how training with MonoLoss changes those results. This is a different measurement and intervention from the original neuron examples.
record.gate_note: The study reports training and evaluation outcomes for SAE latents and added embedding dimensions. Most relevant are the MonoScore and class-purity comparisons, plus qualitative examples across activation strengths. Runtime benchmarks are not results about polysemanticity. Exact per-configuration MonoScore values in Figure 4 and individual scores in Figures 26–28 are not reliably assignable from the flattened figure text.
record.test_reason: Most results concern SAE latents trained on frozen vision-encoder features. These are dictionary features, not the network's own neurons, so they fit no version. The fine-tuning experiment does bear on network neurons: a linear embedding layer is added to ResNet-50 and CLIP-ViT-B/32, and MonoLoss is applied as a regularizer. Without MonoLoss, the units are shown mixing unrelated classes (V1). With MonoLoss, they become coherent and accuracy does not fall (V5). This is a different method aimed at the same question.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors make MonoScore linear-time and use it as a loss (MonoLoss). MonoLoss raises SAE MonoScore for most latents and class purity in all 12 combinations, at some reconstruction cost; the cost is largest for supervised ViT and Vanilla ReLU. Vanilla ReLU on SigLIP2/ImageNet is the one MonoScore decrease. As a fine-tuning regularizer, it gives up to 0.6% ImageNet accuracy gains with near-zero overhead. They note that purity reflects relative gains and that MonoScore depends on the embedding model.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses MonoScore as a batch-wise training objective for SAEs and as a fine-tuning regularizer, rather than merely measuring existing neuron responses. The authors also derive a linear-time computation for the metric.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by encoder and SAE architecture; the paper reports Vanilla ReLU with SigLIP2 on ImageNet-1K as a slight MonoScore exception, and reports a reconstruction/interpretability trade-off. In its supplementary profiles, stronger MonoLoss can reduce the number of nonzero-scoring latents, with the extent depending on encoder.

fits_no_version.finding: In SAEs trained on CLIP, SigLIP2 and ViT features, MonoLoss raises class purity in all 12 encoder–SAE combinations and MonoScore in nearly all. Vanilla ReLU SAEs stay near zero purity, and MonoScore drops slightly for SigLIP2–Vanilla on ImageNet. MonoLoss costs reconstruction R², most for supervised ViT and Vanilla ReLU.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Monosemanticity of SAE dictionary latents depends on SAE architecture and can be raised by a monosemanticity loss at modest reconstruction cost.

fits_no_version.finding: Baseline SAE latents look coherent at top activations but mix unrelated concepts at weaker activations (Figures 3, 5, 6–25).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether an SAE latent looks monosemantic depends on which part of its activation range is inspected.

record.problems: No error bars or uncertainty estimates are reported for the core comparisons. Class purity depends on ImageNet labels and is not a direct semantic ground-truth measure; the authors acknowledge label bias and dependence of MonoScore on the embedding model. Qualitative examples are selected examples rather than a full accounting of individual units.
record.rows_left_out: The 24 separate per-configuration MonoScore values in Figure 4 and the per-latent MonoScore profiles in Figures 26–28 are omitted because the flattened figure text does not reliably assign exact values to each condition; their reported aggregate trend and exception are recorded in mono-aggregate. Task accuracy values from Table 2 and the many separate qualitative examples in Appendix C and Figures 30–40 are omitted to stay within the row limit and prioritize direct monosemanticity results. The paper's runtime comparisons are not claim-relevant.

untested.parts: InceptionV1 or native backbone neurons; how common polysemantic units are (only selected examples from an added layer).
Activation function or architecture of the network itself; any quantitative share or mean MonoScore for the fine-tuned layers; applying the loss to native layers.
For network neurons, neither activation-range dependence nor alternative explanation scoring was examined.

missing.what: Fine-tuning accuracy with versus without MonoLoss per lambda (bears on the V5 performance cost). Declared as left out in rows_left_out, but needed for V5.
Authors report that MonoLoss on the backbone's native last layer caused overfitting, so an extra layer was added.
Numeric MonoScore and active-count for fine-tuned CLIP dimensions, e.g. 0.795 with 6181 active versus 0.848 with 51 active.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked SAE latents to neuron-level versions; I unlinked them. The claims concern network neurons, and SAE latents are a learned dictionary over features. Fine-tuning evidence is only selected qualitative examples from an added layer. No quantitative polysemanticity measure is reported for those layers, and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: It studies SAE latents and added embedding dimensions, not native InceptionV1 neurons or the cited neuron 4e:55.
Transformer language models and token/context responses.
Whether superposition or feature-to-neuron capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.

The study compares SAE architectures and encoders and tests a training regularizer; it does not isolate the causal contribution of activation function, architecture, or regularization separately. It tests task performance in the reported fine-tuning settings, not performance across all model types.
Whether apparently unrelated mixtures in canonical neurons share a feature the network uses or are artifacts of interpretation.
The study compares activation strengths and uses MonoScore, but does not systematically compare alternative explanation-scoring methods.
